analysis.one_liner: Sets minimum seat and bathroom standards for airlines, refunds broken amenities, and rebooking rights on other airlines after long delays.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a vote; it sat in the House Transportation Committee until the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have directed the Transportation Department to set minimum standards for airline seat and bathroom size, require refunds for broken in-flight amenities, fine airlines up to $1,000 per passenger for false weather excuses or tarmac-rule violations, force disclosure of fees not included in the ticket price, and restore the old Rule 240 so a passenger on a flight delayed three hours or more could switch to another airline. It was referred to the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee and its Aviation Subcommittee, and no further action was ever taken.
analysis.who_benefits: Airline passengers. They would gain guaranteed refunds when promised amenities don't work, automatic rebooking on a competing airline after a three-hour controllable delay, advance notice of cancellations, plain-language disclosure of fees and their rights, a 12-month warning before frequent-flyer devaluations, and minimum seat and lavatory standards set in consultation with health agencies and passenger advocates.

how_it_helps.text: Requires airlines to refund up to 10 percent of the ticket price when in-flight amenities like TVs, headphones, or Wi-Fi are broken, and to fully refund any paid service not delivered.

Restores the reciprocity rule (Rule 240), letting passengers on flights cancelled or delayed three or more hours use their ticket on another airline to the same or nearby destination, and requires a replacement ticket on another carrier within 24 hours for controllable delays.

Imposes $1,000-per-passenger fines for false 'force majeure' claims — the bill explicitly excludes understaffing, lack of aircraft, or higher operating costs from counting as beyond the airline's control — and for violations of tarmac delay rules requiring food, water, and operable lavatories.
Directs the Transportation Department to issue minimum standards for seat and bathroom size, safety, and health within 180 days, in consultation with OSHA, the CDC, and passenger advocacy groups.
Requires conspicuous advance disclosure of fees not included in airfare and bans fees more than 200 percent above the airline's cost of providing the service.
Requires airlines to maintain reserve staffing and equipment plans aimed at keeping controllable cancellations under 2 percent and controllable delays under 15 percent, with fines for noncompliance.

analysis.who_pays: Passenger airlines, which would face fines, refund mandates, fee limits, rebooking obligations, staffing and equipment reserve plans, and annual performance reporting to the FAA. Some of those costs would likely be passed on through ticket prices.

drawbacks.text: Mandates such as reserve staffing plans, fee caps, and cross-airline rebooking impose compliance and operating costs on carriers, which airlines typically pass through to passengers in the form of higher fares or fewer optional services.

The fee cap — no fee above 200 percent of the airline's cost — would limit pricing flexibility for optional services like Wi-Fi and baggage handling, potentially reducing investment in those amenities.

The bill sets specific performance targets (fewer than 2 percent cancellations, fewer than 15 percent delays from controllable causes) without addressing how airlines would absorb the operational cost of hitting them, a design an honest supporter would acknowledge is rigid.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For passengers the protections are concrete and directly aimed at documented pain points — false delay excuses, broken Wi-Fi, shrinking seats, surprise fees, and stranded tarmac waits. The costs fall on airlines, and some portion reaches travelers through fares, but the bill's complaint hotline funding and arbitration system are built to give passengers an actual avenue to enforce the new rights. The main weakness is rigid one-size-fits-all performance targets rather than the protections themselves.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee and its Aviation Subcommittee in July 2017 and never came back out, dying when the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Mike Thompson (D-CA) introduced the Airline Passenger Protection Act of 2017 on July 14, 2017.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure the day it was introduced, and the next day to its Subcommittee on Aviation.
The bill had a single cosponsor and no further legislative action of any kind was recorded after the subcommittee referral, through the end of the 115th Congress on January 3, 2019.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The passenger airlines are better off: no seat or bathroom minimums, no cross-airline rebooking duty, no fee cap, and no new fines took effect. Passengers continue to rely on whatever voluntary policies carriers choose.

for.name: Rep. Mike Thompson
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to committee.

against.name: Rep. Bill Shuster
against.role: Chair, House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee
against.what_they_did: The committee he chaired took no action on the bill after referral; no markup or floor vote was ever scheduled.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken; the only recorded support was a Democratic sponsor and one Democratic cosponsor, and no Republican is on record either way.

industries.note: The bill would have fined carriers up to $1,000 per passenger for false delay excuses and tarmac-rule violations, required refunds for broken amenities, capped ancillary fees at 200 percent of cost, forced cross-airline rebooking after long controllable delays, and mandated reserve staffing plans. Blocking the bill preserved carriers' discretion over seats, fees, refunds, and rebooking.

industries.industry: Travel technology and in-flight amenity providers
industries.note: Refund requirements for Wi-Fi, entertainment, and other in-air purchases would pressure carriers to keep those services working, cutting both ways for the vendors behind them.
